questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless indurated ulcer on his penis for 3 weeks. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the serous exudate shows motile spirochetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents as a painless, indurated (Hunterian) chancre with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy demonstrating Treponema pallidum (motile spirochetes) confirms the diagnosis. Chancroid is painful; LGV causes groove sign; granuloma inguinale shows Donovan bodies.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops tense bullae on sun-exposed areas. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blister with neutrophils. DIF shows IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. She has antibodies against type VII collagen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous SLE is a rare vesiculobullous eruption in SLE patients with antibodies against type VII collagen (same target as EBA), occurring in the context of SLE. DIF shows IgG/IgM/IgA and complement at the BMZ. Neutrophilic infiltrate and photosensitivity in an SLE patient clinch bullous SLE over EBA.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous plaque on the foot for 2 years. Biopsy shows thick-walled, brown, septate fungal cells (Medlar bodies) within the tissue. Which organism is LEAST likely to be causative?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous fungi: Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa, Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, and Exophiala jeanselmei. Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis, showing cigar-shaped yeast in tissue, not sclerotic bodies.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a pearly, telangiectatic nodule on his nose that has grown over 6 months. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests. Histology reveals peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with retraction artifact. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Wide local excision with 1 cm margin
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone, high-risk site) is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, offering the highest cure rate with maximal tissue conservation. Wide excision is for truncal BCC; imiquimod for superficial BCC; cryotherapy for low-risk superficial lesions.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on his trunk and a thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. Biopsy shows epithelioid cell granulomas with perineural and intraneural infiltration. What is the leprosy type?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT): few well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic patches, thickened peripheral nerves, negative SSS (paucibacillary), and biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with perineural and intraneural involvement — the nerve is virtually destroyed by the granuloma.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and dysphagia for 5 years. Anti-centromere antibodies are positive. Which complication is she MOST at risk for?
questions.exp: This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc / CREST syndrome). Anti-centromere antibodies are strongly associated with lcSSc and specifically with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Pulmonary fibrosis and renal crisis are more typical of diffuse cutaneous SSc (anti-Scl-70). PAH is the leading cause of death in lcSSc.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male with CD4 count of 80 cells/μL develops crops of umbilicated papules on the face, neck, and trunk with a central keratinous core. What is the cornerstone of management?
opts: HAART plus physical destruction of lesions
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus) occurs extensively in immunocompromised patients. In HIV, the cornerstone is immune reconstitution with HAART; physical destruction (cryotherapy, curettage) addresses individual lesions. Acyclovir is for herpesviruses; fluconazole for fungi; griseofulvin for dermatophytes.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male has a scarring alopecia on the scalp with follicular plugging and dyspigmentation. Biopsy shows interface dermatitis with periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. DIF shows IgM and C3 deposits at the BMZ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) of the scalp causes scarring alopecia with follicular plugging, dyspigmentation, and telangiectasia. Biopsy shows interface dermatitis and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. DIF shows lupus band (IgG, IgM, C3) at the BMZ in lesional skin.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male develops a tender suppurative inguinal bubo 2 weeks after a self-healing painless genital ulcer. Frei test is positive. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. It presents with a transient painless primary ulcer followed by tender inguinal bubo (groove sign when Poupart's ligament is involved). Frei test is positive but non-specific. Treated with doxycycline for 21 days.

questions.q: A neonate develops flaccid bullae and positive Nikolsky sign within 48 hours of birth. The mother has a staphylococcal infection. Gram stain of the bulla fluid is sterile. What toxin is responsible?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A and B (ET-A, ET-B)
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serine proteases) produced by S. aureus phage group II. These toxins cleave desmoglein-1 in the granular layer, causing superficial blistering. Bulla fluid is sterile. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome; alpha toxin causes deeper tissue damage.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with psoriasis has painful DIP joint involvement with nail pitting, onycholysis, and sausage digits. Rheumatoid factor is negative. Which pattern of psoriatic arthritis does he have?
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis has 5 patterns (Moll and Wright): asymmetric oligoarthritis (most common), DIP predominant, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans, and spondyloarthropathy. DIP predominant pattern is almost exclusive to psoriatic arthritis and is strongly associated with nail disease.

questions.q: During photopatch testing, a patient reacts to a substance only at the irradiated site. The reaction persists for 6 weeks despite avoidance of the photosensitizer and sunlight. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.exp: Persistent light reaction (PLR) occurs when photoallergic contact dermatitis persists despite removal of the causative photosensitizer and sunlight avoidance, due to persistent delayed hypersensitivity to UV radiation itself. Actinic reticuloid is the most severe end of the chronic actinic dermatitis spectrum with pseudolymphomatous histology.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with pruritic, symmetric papulovesicular eruption on elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction papillary tips. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. DIF shows granular IgA at the papillary dermis tips (pathognomonic). Treatment: gluten-free diet (long-term) + dapsone for rapid symptom control. Prednisolone is ineffective. Doxycycline + nicotinamide is used in bullous pemphigoid. Rituximab is for pemphigus.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man has multiple warty papules on his back with a waxy, stuck-on appearance. Dermoscopy shows comedo-like openings and milia-like cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Seborrheic keratosis is the most common benign epithelial tumour in the elderly, with a waxy, stuck-on appearance. Dermoscopy shows comedo-like openings, milia-like cysts, and hairpin vessels. Sudden onset of multiple lesions (Leser-Trélat sign) may indicate internal malignancy.

questions.q: A child with blistering at birth that improves with age develops diffuse hyperkeratosis. Electron microscopy shows clumped tonofilaments in suprabasal keratinocytes. Gene mutation is in KRT1 or KRT10. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (EHK / bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) is caused by mutations in KRT1 or KRT10 (suprabasal keratins). EM shows keratin filament clumping and perinuclear shells. Blistering in infancy improves with age but is replaced by warty hyperkeratosis. EBS involves KRT5/KRT14 (basal); lamellar ichthyosis involves TGM1.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic male presents with a rapidly expanding necrotic lesion on his scrotum and perineum with foul-smelling discharge and crepitus. He is febrile and hemodynamically unstable. What is the immediate management?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a synergistic polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the genitalia — a surgical emergency. Immediate management: urgent and aggressive surgical debridement (cornerstone) plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes. Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive. Antifungals alone are insufficient.

questions.q: Under Wood's lamp (365 nm UV), bright green fluorescence of affected hair shafts in tinea capitis is produced by which organisms?
questions.exp: Microsporum species (M. canis, M. audouinii, M. ferrugineum) cause ectothrix infection with bright green fluorescence due to pteridine metabolites. Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum (endothrix) do not fluoresce. T. schoenleinii (favus) shows dull pale green fluorescence. Epidermophyton does not cause tinea capitis.

questions.q: A 32-week pregnant woman develops intensely pruritic urticarial plaques starting on the abdomen. DIF shows linear C3 at the BMZ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigoid gestationis (herpes gestationis) is an autoimmune bullous disorder of pregnancy. DIF shows linear C3 (and sometimes IgG) at the BMZ. Associated with BP180 antibodies. Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PUPPP) spares the umbilicus and has no DIF deposits. Cholestasis presents with jaundice and elevated bile acids.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man develops a nodule on his finger after pruning rose bushes, followed by a linear chain of nodules along his forearm following the lymphatics. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii), classically following thorn inoculation, shows sporotrichoid spread (nodules along lymphatics). Treatment of choice: itraconazole 200 mg/day for 3-6 months. SSKI is an older alternative but less tolerated. Amphotericin B is reserved for systemic/disseminated disease.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student has recurrent grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her lip, recurring with stress and fever. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the mechanism of recurrence?
opts: Reinfection from an external source each time
Latency in dorsal root ganglion with reactivation along the same dermatome
Autoimmune T-cell destruction of epithelial cells
questions.exp: HSV-1 establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion after primary infection. Reactivation triggers (stress, UV, fever, immunosuppression) cause virus to travel anterograde along sensory neurons to the skin, causing recurrent herpes labialis at the same site — the hallmark of herpetic latency and reactivation.

questions.q: A 68-year-old male has a 4 cm pigmented lesion on his cheek with variegated colour (tan, brown, black) and slow growth over 10 years arising from a lentigo maligna background. Biopsy shows atypical melanocytes along the basal layer of sun-damaged skin. What type of melanoma is this?
questions.exp: Lentigo maligna melanoma (LMM) arises from lentigo maligna in chronically sun-damaged skin of elderly patients, most often on the face, with the longest radial growth phase. Histology shows atypical melanocytes along the DEJ of photodamaged skin (solar elastosis). SSM shows pagetoid spread; nodular melanoma lacks radial growth phase; ALM is on acral sites.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child has silvery-white scales encasing hair shafts proximally that can be slid off without breaking the hair. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pityriasis amiantacea presents with thick, adherent, asbestos-like scales encasing hair shafts proximally, which slide up the shaft when removed. It is a reaction pattern seen in psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, eczema — not a specific disease. No fluorescence under Wood's lamp. White piedra shows soft nodules; pediculosis shows nits cemented to shafts.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine develops grey-brown hyperpigmentation on her skin. Biopsy shows golden-brown granules in macrophages positive for both Perl's Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson stains. What is the nature of these granules?
opts: A complex of melanin, haemosiderin, and drug metabolite
questions.exp: Antimalarial drugs cause pigmentation that is a complex of melanin, haemosiderin, and drug metabolite. It stains positively with both Perl's (iron) and Fontana-Masson (melanin), distinguishing it from pure melanin (negative Perl's) or haemosiderin alone. Common sites: face, shins, hard palate.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with varicose veins develops bilateral lower leg eczema that spreads to his thighs. He has been using neomycin-containing wound dressings. Patch testing shows ++ reaction to neomycin sulphate. What is the complete diagnosis?
questions.exp: This patient has stasis dermatitis complicated by allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to neomycin (a common sensitizer in wound care), confirmed by positive patch test. Secondary spread to distant sites is autosensitization (id reaction). Neomycin ACD with id reaction in varicose eczema is a classic combination.

questions.q: In leprosy, the Mitsuda reaction (late lepromin test at 28 days) correlates best with which of the following?
opts: Past or present infection with M. leprae
questions.exp: The Mitsuda (late lepromin) reaction reflects CMI to M. leprae — positive in tuberculoid leprosy (strong CMI) and negative in lepromatous leprosy (anergic). It is not diagnostic (many healthy individuals are positive) but indicates the host's immune response. Antibodies to PGL-1 correlate with bacillary load.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman develops diffuse non-scarring hair loss 3 months after delivery of a healthy baby. Trichogram shows >20% telogen hairs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Postpartum telogen effluvium occurs 2-4 months after delivery due to the synchronous shift of anagen hairs (maintained by high oestrogen during pregnancy) into telogen after delivery. Trichogram shows >20% telogen hairs. It is self-limiting and resolves by 6-12 months. Anagen effluvium is caused by chemotherapy and causes immediate diffuse shedding.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male has a 3 cm cystic lesion with cheesy contents on his forearm. Histology shows a wall lined by stratified squamous epithelium WITH a granular layer and lamellated keratin. What is this lesion?
questions.exp: Epidermoid cyst is lined by true stratified squamous epithelium WITH a granular cell layer, containing lamellated keratin. Trichilemmal cysts (most common on scalp) LACK a granular layer and show abrupt trichilemmal keratinization with calcification. Dermoid cysts contain adnexal structures. Milia are tiny epidermoid cysts <2 mm.

questions.q: A patient with pemphigus vulgaris on dapsone develops Heinz bodies on peripheral smear and fatigue. Methemoglobin level is 8%. What is the mechanism of dapsone-induced haemolysis?
questions.exp: Dapsone is metabolized by N-hydroxylation to hydroxylamine, which causes oxidative damage to haemoglobin, leading to methaemoglobinaemia and Heinz body haemolytic anaemia. This is dose-dependent and more severe in G6PD-deficient patients. It is a pharmacotoxic, not immune-mediated, mechanism.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with flat-topped, violaceous polygonal papules on her wrists. Oral mucosa shows Wickham's striae. Biopsy shows saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ, and Civatte bodies. What is the autoimmune mechanism?
opts: Type IV hypersensitivity (CD8+ T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes)
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder. CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes attack basal keratinocytes, causing lichenoid interface dermatitis. Civatte bodies are apoptotic keratinocytes. This is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. Oral Wickham's striae are due to focal hypergranulosis.

questions.q: During a punch biopsy closure on the medial forearm, in which direction should the long axis of the ellipse be oriented for best cosmetic outcome?
opts: Horizontally, perpendicular to the lines of skin tension
Randomly, as punch biopsy scars are always circular
Along the relaxed skin tension lines (Langer's lines), running longitudinally on the forearm
Diagonally at 45 degrees to reduce puckering
questions.exp: When a punch biopsy is converted to an ellipse for primary closure, the long axis should be oriented along the relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs/Langer's lines) to minimize tension and achieve optimal cosmesis. On the medial forearm, RSTLs run longitudinally. Orientation perpendicular to RSTLs results in a wide, hypertrophic scar.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with painful erythematous nodules on his shins bilaterally. He has a history of sarcoidosis. Biopsy of the nodule shows a septal panniculitis with no vasculitis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (EN) is the most common panniculitis, presenting as tender erythematous nodules on the shins. Histology shows septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis — the hallmark. Associated with sarcoidosis, streptococcal infection, TB, IBD, and drugs. Erythema induratum (lobular panniculitis with vasculitis) occurs on the calves, often in women with TB.
